one_liner: C++ minimal perfect hash: RecSplit with cuckoo-hashing leaves, building 1.56-1.58 bits/key MPHFs 15-160x faster than RecSplit/SIMDRecSplit.
what_it_does: Builds a static minimal perfect hash function (MPHF) over a fixed key set of std::string (vector/span) or pre-hashed 128-bit values: each of the n keys maps to a distinct integer in [0, n). The API has the same shape as sux RecSplit: `shockhash::ShockHash<LEAF_SIZE, ROTATION_FITTING> f(keys, bucket_size, num_threads)` then `f(key)`, with the SIMD variant `SIMDShockHash` and the newer bipartite `ShockHash2` / `ShockHash2Flat` in the same repo. You cannot insert or delete keys, and there is no membership check, so a key outside the build set gets an arbitrary index.
how_it_is_fast: It keeps RecSplit's recursive splitting tree but replaces the brute-force bijection search in each leaf (about e^n seed trials) with ShockHash ('small, heavily overloaded cuckoo hash tables'): each seed gives every key two candidate cells in an n-cell table, and the seed is accepted if the random graph is a pseudoforest, meaning the table can be filled completely by cuckoo insertion. A 1-bit BuRR ribbon retrieval structure records which of the two cells each key uses, and this cuts the expected trials to (e/2)^n·poly(n), almost 2^n fewer, so leaves can have n=30-58 instead of RecSplit's ~8-16. Most seeds are rejected early by a bit-mask filter that checks every cell is hit; the filter runs in registers with AVX2/AVX-512 SIMD, and rotation fitting tries n cyclic rotations of half the keys per hash evaluation.
when_to_use: Static key sets (millions to hundreds of millions of string keys) where the MPHF must sit close to the 1.44 bits/key lower bound. Table 1 configurations reach 1.52-1.58 bits/key.

You already use RecSplit or SIMDRecSplit at b=2000 with leaf 14-16 and build time is the bottleneck. At matched space, ShockHash-RS builds in 787-1,805 ns/key; RecSplit and SIMDRecSplit take 11,749-137,902 ns/key.
Processes that build the function once and keep it in RAM, where a ~115 ns query is acceptable. For example, 10M keys with n=30, b=2000 is about 8 s of single-threaded construction.
x86-64 Linux with GCC 11+ and AVX2 or AVX-512, using SIMDShockHash with rotation fitting. This is the configuration the paper measured.
To go below ~1.52 bits/key, use `ShockHash2` (bipartite ShockHash, arXiv 2310.14959) from the same repo. Its abstract reports 1.489 bits/key for 10M keys in about half an hour.
when_not_to_use: Lookup latency is the constraint. In the same Table 1, queries take 114-118 ns; PTHash takes 20-34 ns and FMPHGO 53-69 ns, at 2.2-4.4 bits/key.
You need to save the function to disk and load it later. ShockHash, SIMDShockHash and ShockHash2 have no serialization API (sux RecSplit has `operator<<`/`operator>>`), so every run must rebuild.
Dynamic key sets, or code that must detect foreign keys. The function is static and returns an arbitrary index for keys it was not built on, so you need a separate key or fingerprint store.

Clang, MSVC, Windows, macOS or ARM toolchains. CI covers only GCC 11/12/13 on Ubuntu, the code uses `<experimental/simd>`, raw x86 intrinsics in the SIMD path and `1ul` shifts of up to 60 bits, and CMake links Intel TBB.
The most compact ShockHash-RS setting (n=58, 1.523 bits/key) costs 111,593 ns/key, about 19 minutes single-threaded for 10M keys. The newer ConsensusRecSplit reports getting much closer to the bound.

integration.form: shared lib (CMake add_subdirectory of the repo with submodules; header-only INTERFACE target plus compiled shared libs ShockHash2Precompiled, Ips2raShockHashSorter, SimpleRibbon, RibbonSorter)
integration.dependencies: Git submodules: sux (ByteHamster fork), SimpleRibbon (BuRR, ips2ra, tlx), tlx, ByteHamster/Util (pasta-bit-vector), and vectorclass (SIMD variant only). Intel TBB from the system (CI installs libtbb-dev). CMake 3.25+.
integration.min_toolchain: C++20; GCC 11+ (CI tests GCC 11/12/13; a commit notes GCC 10 lacks <experimental/simd>); CMake 3.25
integration.platforms: Tested only on Linux x86-64 (Ubuntu CI). SIMDShockHash needs AVX2, uses AVX-512 when available, and must be compiled with -DSIMD. Clang, macOS, Windows and aarch64 are not documented. The code assumes 64-bit unsigned long, and keys beyond 2^32 need __int128 support.
integration.thread_safety: Construction can use several threads through the num_threads constructor argument (the paper's benchmarks used 1). Thread safety of concurrent queries is not documented. `ShockHash::operator()` is non-const, while `ShockHash2::operator()` is const.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the constructor (keys, bucket_size) and operator()(key) match sux RecSplit, but the namespace differs, LEAF_SIZE goes up to 60 (128 for ShockHash2), there is an extra num_threads argument, there is no stream serialization, and the returned indices differ.

gotchas: Duplicate keys make the constructor loop forever. This is documented in SIMDShockHash's doc comment, as in sux RecSplit. Deduplicate keys before building.
MAX_BUCKET_SIZE is 3000, and the header says it 'works with high probability up to average bucket size ~2000'. Only an assert guards the limit, so keep bucket_size at 2000 or below.

CMake compiles Ips2raShockHashSorter and ShockHash2Precompiled with -march=native unconditionally, and the ShockHashSIMD target passes -march=native on to consumers. Binaries may not run on CPUs older than the build host.

The Table 1 numbers come from `SIMDShockHash<n, true>` (SIMD plus rotation fitting, via the MPHF-Experiments ShockHashContender). The README example `ShockHash<30, false>` is the slower scalar path without rotation fitting. SIMDShockHash stops with #error unless built with -DSIMD (link the ShockHashSIMD target).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over RecSplit (sux) or SimdRecSplit when you want 1.52-1.59 bits/key without their 11,749-137,902 ns/key builds, and can accept up to ~20% slower queries (114-118 vs 97-108 ns) and no serialization. Prefer ConsensusRecSplit (same group, 2025; 1.4448 bits/key on 100M keys in about an hour) for minimum space, and PTHash or SicHash when 2-4.4 bits/key is acceptable in return for builds and queries several times faster.
verified_claims_summary: The paper's Table 1 (arXiv 2308.09561v2) measures 10M random strings of length 10-50, single-threaded, compiled with GCC 11.2.0 -O3 -march=native on an Intel i7-11700 with AVX-512, running SIMDShockHash with rotation fitting. At ~1.56 bits/key, ShockHash-RS n=39 builds at 1,805 ns/key against SIMDRecSplit's 137,902 ns/key (~76x). At ~1.585 bits/key, n=30 builds at 787 ns/key against sux RecSplit's 125,521 ns/key (~160x), but only ~15x against SIMDRecSplit's 11,749 ns/key. Queries are 114-118 ns against 97-108 ns.
status_note: Stale: the last commit was 2025-03-31, there are no releases or tags, no GitHub issues have ever been filed, and it has 15 stars. The research code uses GPL-3.0 with the GCC Runtime Library Exception, which the README says permits use like libstdc++. Vendoring it means vendoring six submodules and depending on system TBB.
